UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

        Maryland Office of People’s                 )
        Counsel                                     )
                                                    )
        v.                                          )                Docket No. EL26-63-000
                                                    )
        PJM Interconnection, LLC                    )
                                                    )

      COMMENTS OF THE OFFICE OF THE ILLINOIS ATTORNEY GENERAL

        Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (the “Commission”

or “FERC”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, the Office of the Illinois Attorney General 1 (“IL

OAG”) submits these comments in response to the complaint filed by the Maryland Office of

People’s Counsel (“Maryland OPC”) on May 7, 2026. In its complaint, Maryland OPC requested

that the Commission find that PJM Interconnection, LLC’s (“PJM”) current cost allocation

methods for baseline transmission upgrades are unjust and unreasonable. 2 Maryland OPC argues

that current cost allocation methodology for baseline transmission upgrades in PJM shifts onto

Maryland customers transmission costs driven by large loads elsewhere in the PJM footprint that

do not benefit Maryland. 3

        IL OAG represents the People of the State of Illinois and their interest in receiving reliable

electric services at the least possible cost. 4 IL OAG is vested by Illinois law with “the power and

duty on behalf of the people of the State to intervene in, initiate, enforce, and defend all legal

proceedings on matters relating to the provision, marketing, and sale of electric … service


1
  The Office of the Illinois Attorney General has moved to intervene in this proceeding. See (doc-less) Motion to
Intervene of the Office of the Illinois Attorney General, Docket No. EL26-63-000 (filed May 15, 2026)
(“Intervention”).
2
  Complaint Requesting Fast Track Processing of the Maryland Office of People’s Counsel., Maryland Office of
People’s Counsel v. PJM Interconnection, LLC., Docket No. EL26-63-000 (filed May 7, 2026) (“Complaint”). See
also Notice Granting Extension of Time, Docket No. EL26-63-000 (filed May 22, 2026).
3
  Complaint, supra note 2, at 2.
4
  See 15 ILCS 205/6.5(c), (d); Intervention, supra note 1.

                                                        1
 whenever the Attorney General determines that such action is necessary to promote or protect the

rights and interests of all Illinois citizens[.]” 5 The northern portion of Illinois, including the City

of Chicago, comprises the ComEd zone of the PJM footprint,6 and the more than 4 million retail

customers located in the ComEd zone pay FERC-approved transmission rates each month.

Therefore, the People of the State of Illinois have an interest in addressing the transmission cost

allocation issues raised by Maryland as part of the broader regulatory discussion surrounding the

impact of large load customers. 7 IL OAG seeks to ensure that Illinois residents do not pay for

transmission upgrades caused by and which solely benefit large load customers.

        IL OAG supports the Maryland OPC complaint, which identified serious issues with the

socialization of data center costs through the current allocation methods for baseline transmission

projects. While costs caused by data centers can be assigned to those data centers in the way

Maryland OPC suggests in its complaint, FERC policy regarding transmission cost allocation in

general needs to be updated so that large load customers that drive expensive transmission

upgrades pay both the incremental connection and upgrade costs they cause and the embedded

cost to deliver electric service to them and receive the other benefits of the national electricity grid.

                                                COMMENTS

        Data center growth is driving massive investments in new transmission infrastructure. PJM

forecasts 32 GW of peak load growth by 2030, and 30 GW of that growth is being driven by data



5
  15 ILCS 205/6.5(c).
6
  Illinois ratepayers are served by two Regional Transmission Organizations, Midcontinent Independent System
Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) and PJM. Central and Southern Illinois are encompassed by MISO Local Resource Zone 4
and a small portion of Northwest Illinois is included in MISO Local Resource Zone 1 See MISO Tariff, Attachment
VV, Map of Local Resource Zone Boundaries, https://docs.misoenergy.org/miso12-legalcontent/Attachment_VV_
_MAP_of_Local_Resource_Zone_Boundaries.pdf. The service area of Commonwealth Edison Company, the load
serving entity for Illinois electricity customers in Northern Illinois, is encompassed by PJM’s ComEd Zone. See PJM
Open Access Transmission Tariff, Attachment J, PJM Transmission Zones, https://agreements.pjm.com/oatt/4443.
7
  See, e.g., Notice Inviting Comments, Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System, Docket
No. RM26-4 (Oct. 27, 2025); Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act re: PJM
Interconnection, L.L.C. et al., Docket No. EL26-67 (June 18, 2026).

                                                        2
 centers. 8 In the ComEd zone, large load growth has been estimated at 11 GW of new demand by

2035. 9 These large loads, both in Illinois and throughout the PJM region, are driving new

transmission investments to serve them. In the previous three PJM Regional Transmission

Expansion Plan (“RTEP”) procurement windows, PJM authorized baseline project investment of

$22 billion. 10 To the extent that non-large load customers do not benefit from those transmission

upgrades, they should not be required to pay the costs of those upgrades.

       While IL OAG largely supports Maryland OPC’s proposals as a step in the right direction

to avoid cross-subsidization, those proposals do not reach the heart of the issue. As explained

below, transmission cost allocation issues stemming from large load will persist in PJM because

of the historical presumption that the incremental and embedded cost to serve large load are

duplicative. Failing to charge both, or offering a credit for one against the other, as Maryland OPC

proposes, will always result in other customers subsidizing the large load. IL OAG recommends

that FERC reverse its policy prohibiting “and” pricing and order PJM to allow transmission owners

to charge large load customers for both the incremental and embedded cost of service via a Cost

Recovery Agreement between the transmission owner, the Eligible Customer, and the large load.

This should apply not only to baseline transmission upgrades as Maryland OPC requests, but to

supplemental projects as well.

I.     PJM’s current transmission cost allocation rules unjustly burden Illinois customers

       A. Current Cost Allocation Rules for Baseline and Supplemental Projects

       PJM divides transmission projects into three main categories: baseline projects, network

upgrades, and supplemental projects.11 Baseline projects “ensure compliance with national and


8
  David Mills, Letter to PJM Stakeholders, PJM (Aug. 8, 2025).
9
  PJM Interconnection, 2026 Long-Term Load Forecast Supplement, February 2026.
10
   See 2022 W3 RTEP, TEAC, Recommendations to the PJM Board White Paper (Dec. 2023), 2024 W1 RTEP TEAC
Recommendations to the PJM Board White Paper (Feb. 2025), 2025 W1 RTEP Recommendations to the PJM Board
White Paper (Feb. 2026).
11
   PJM Interconnection, RTEP: Planning for Long-Term Transmission Needs, January 2025.

                                                  3
 regional reliability standards.”12 These projects are need-based 13 and driven by the RTEP process.

Network upgrades refer to equipment enhancements needed for new customers seeking long-term

transmission service and connection to the grid. 14 These projects typically address interconnecting

generators and merchant transmission facilities. 15 Finally, supplemental projects are “transmission

expansions or enhancements by transmission owners to address local reliability needs.” 16 Unlike

the other transmission projects, PJM does not affirmatively determine whether there is a need for

supplemental projects; PJM merely “evaluates these projects to ensure they do not cause reliability

problems on the regional grid.” 17

        Baseline projects have a “hybrid methodology” for allocating costs of 500kV+ lines and

necessary lower-voltage facilities. The methodology assigns 50 percent of costs via load-ratio

share and 50 percent through solution-based distribution factor (“DFAX”). If a project falls below

500 kV, then the solution-based DFAX method applies. The Load-Ratio share component allocates

costs on what is described as a “postage stamp” method. The method allocates costs in proportion

to each PJM zone’s annual coincident peak load. Solution-based DFAX is a power flow model. It

models “how electricity will flow across a new transmission facility at moments of peak grid use

(i.e., at ‘peak load’), and assigns costs proportionally, based on the projected use of the facility by

utilities in each ‘zone’ of the PJM grid.” 18 The DFAX models both the amount and direction of

power flows.

13

Public Policy. The PJM Planning Committee looks primarily to these factors when deciding whether there is a need
for a project.

          Supplemental projects have a comparably simple cost allocation methodology.

Supplemental projects within a given zone are allocated directly to that zone. 19 A supplemental

project constructed in the ComEd zone is directly allocated to the ComEd zone. Within PJM,

supplemental projects represent the bulk of transmission costs. The 2024 RTEP identified $820.9

million in supplemental transmission project spending20 while it only included $143.23 million in

baseline projects in ComEd territory. 21

         Maryland OPCs’ complaint acknowledges that it is focused on the cost allocation issues

with baseline transmission projects and not “supplemental [transmission] projects associated with

large-load growth.” 22 Nevertheless, it is necessary to understand these projects because the concern

regarding cross-subsidization of large load customers that Maryland OPC raises with respect to

baseline transmission projects also applies to supplemental projects. Ultimately, both baseline and

supplemental project costs are added to the revenue requirement for the transmission owner in the

relevant zone. 23 Such costs are socialized and collected from transmission customers, who

ultimately recover those costs through retail rates. This system was created under the assumption

that these transmission projects benefit the public broadly, as opposed to a few, discrete users.24

But that assumption no longer holds. The proliferation and unique characteristics of large load

customers have both accelerated the increase in transmission costs and led to a situation where

groups/task-forces/destf/2025/20250918/20250918-item-04---cost-allocation---presentation.pdf.; See also PJM
Open Access Transmission Tariff Attachment M-3.

                                                          5
 existing customers, both between zones and within transmission zones, are bearing costs that they

are not causing and from which they do not benefit.

        B. Cross-Subsidies Between Zones

        The bulk of Maryland OPC’s critique of current cost allocation rules for baseline projects

targets interzonal subsidization, meaning one PJM zone paying for the transmission upgrades

occurring in and benefitting another PJM zone. 25 Maryland OPC notes how both aspects of the

hybrid methodology cost allocation for baseline transmission projects as applied to large loads

violate the cost causation principle and lead to Maryland customers paying for transmission costs

incurred by data centers built in other states.26 Maryland OPC is correct. Both load-ratio share and

solution-based DFAX fail to allocate costs in a way that is remotely “commensurate” with the

benefits that new transmission will create.

        Load-ratio share is an unjust and unreasonable method of assigning costs because it

erroneously assumes that transmission projects built to serve large-load customers benefit the

entire footprint. When load-ratio share as a methodology was developed, many assumed that

facilities of 500kV and higher would only serve massive, interzonal connections capable of

delivering electricity across PJM. 27 That assumption was modified to an extent by FERC in 2013

when it adopted the hybrid methodology, 28 but the assumption no longer holds when applied to

transmission built to serve large loads that can require from 50 MW to 1 GW for a single customer.

        The persistence of the load share ratio as part of the current hybrid methodology for

baseload projects violates cost causation principles. By their design, data centers require high-

26
   See generally, Complaint, supra note 2, at 26.
27
   See Ill. Commerce Comm’n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 474 (7 th Cir. 2009) (ICC I) (“FERC’s stated reasons [for load-
ratio share include]…that everyone benefits from high-capacity transmission facilities because they increase the
reliability of the entire network.”).
28
   See FERC Docket No. ER13-19. See also ICC I, 576 F.3d 470 (disallowing 100% allocation via load-ratio share).

                                                       6
 voltage transmission to connect to the grid. 29 The data center is the beneficiary of that transmission.

This benefit is not spread out to other transmission customers in a zone, much less to the entirety

of PJM. Maryland OPC’s conclusion is correct: “When the driver of transmission investment is in

concentrated large load growth in a discrete geographic area, the rationale for the load-ratio share

component of PJM’s hybrid methodology fails.” 30 Because this methodology guarantees that costs

from distant zones are borne by zones that did not cause those costs and that do not benefit from

that investment, this methodology drives interzonal subsidization, and is therefore unjust and

unreasonable.

        Maryland OPC also correctly identifies that solution-based DFAX is an unjust and

unreasonable way of measuring benefits in the context of large load customers. Maryland OPC

identifies two concerns with solution-based DFAX: First, it does not capture the benefits to

stability that these transmission projects can provide; 31 and second, solution-based DFAX is

undermined by load that fails to materialize. 32 As applied to large loads, the IL OAG agrees with

both criticisms.

        Speculative load and stranded assets have a high potential to drive costs in other zones due

to solution-based DFAX. The frequency of duplicative interconnection requests by large load data

centers has been widely discussed, but difficult to document due to the lack of transparency into

distribution system interconnection.33 What we do know comes from the industry itself. In 2025,

one executive estimated that “[c]onservatively, you’re seeing five to 10 times more interconnection

Testimony of Max Leichtman, ComEd Ex. 3.0 at 4–5 (explaining that large load customers are typically served at

 requests than data centers actually being built.” 34 This uncertainty of what will actually be built

and interconnected will likely rise as industry analyst outlooks 35 and public opinion 36 of the AI

industry worsens. These financial and political pressures expose the possibility that an increasing

number of data centers will fail to take service despite interconnection requests. If transmission

projects are built to serve load that fails to materialize, or even load that is taken offline because

AI demand falls, solution-based DFAX will assign costs to regions where there is existing or

remaining load, which likely will not be where the data center was. The result is the potential for

a catastrophic stranded asset problem that is exacerbated by solution-based DFAX.

        In the recent show cause orders, FERC acknowledged how large load speculation could

result in increased transmission costs for other customers. In Docket No. EL26-67, FERC noted

the following:


                 When a transmission owner constructs network Upgrades to
                 accommodate an Eligible Customer’s request for transmission
                 service on behalf of a large load, those transmission costs will be
                 included in the transmission owner’s revenue requirement. If,
                 however, the Eligible Customer takes less transmission service than
                 anticipated …transmission customers may see an increase in
                 transmission rates. 37

Solution-based DFAX exacerbates this problem and risks raising customer transmission rates by

shifting costs to other transmission owners’ revenue requirements to pay for transmission built for

data centers that fail to materialize or that use less energy than forecasted.

        Illinois customers are currently being asked to subsidize data center growth elsewhere in

PJM. According to data from PJM, the ComEd zone was allocated $50,734,552 in out-of-zone

 baseline project costs. 38 On the other hand, other zones paid approximately $14,588,704 in

baseline project costs originating in the ComEd zone. While it is not exactly known how much of

the $36 million gap is caused by data center growth, it is indicative of the shortcomings of the

current allocation methods. 39

         C. Cross-Subsidies Between Customers Within a Zone

         PJM’s current cost allocation method is also unjust and unreasonable because there is no

mechanism for ensuring existing customers within a zone do not subsidize infrastructure from

which they largely do not derive benefits. Although Maryland OPC’s complaint does not primarily

address intrazonal allocation issues, those failures follow from the same issues the complaint

identifies in the interzonal context. Because large load customers are disproportionately driving

and benefitting from transmission costs, but such costs are pooled together and socialized to all

customers within the zone, existing ratepayers are effectively subsidizing large loads. 40 While

historically transmission upgrades were designed to benefit large numbers of customers, today

large loads that require as much power as a medium sized city are driving transmission costs and

ratepayers have no protection from costs that stem from those extraordinary large load customers.

         Both supplemental and baseline projects built to serve large loads are all but guaranteed to

burden non-large load customers under PJM’s current cost allocation methods. Transmission

customers are charged the Network Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”) rate multiplied by

location, and in an easily accessible format that is searchable and allows users to filter the data, that identifies the
Network Upgrades that are needed to accommodate requests for transmission service by Eligible Customers on behalf
of large loads, and the costs of those Network Upgrades.” The IL OAG is supportive of FERC’s efforts to remedy this
information asymmetry.
40

are pooled together under the category of ‘RTEP baseline reliability upgrades’ and socialized.”)

transmission owner’s annual transmission revenue requirement ($/year) by transmission zone’s

coincident peak load (MW). The current ComEd annual transmission revenue requirement is

$970,989,028,41 resulting in a current NITS rate of $46,876 per MW-day. 42 Data center load can

vary, but if we suppose that a data center seeks to interconnect a 200 MW load, then, assuming the

center consumes all 200 MW at peak (and does not use demand response tools), the incremental

cost must be less than $9.35 million in order to not raise the NITS rate for all transmission

customers. In a state-level proceeding, a witness for IL OAG analyzed seven supplemental projects

associated with large loads that were submitted to PJM and found that the average cost per project

would be approximately $84 million and the total revenue requirement impact would be $2.1

billion over 40 years. 43 IL OAG’s witness further found that the 10-year revenue guarantees sought

by ComEd in that docket would put existing customers at risk of bearing a nearly $900 million

cost shift.

        FERC has already acknowledged that this dynamic is unjust and unreasonable. In the PJM

show cause order, FERC “preliminarily [found] that PJM’s tariff appears to be unjust and

unreasonable because it lacks adequate mechanisms to mitigate the risk of cost shifting among

transmission customers.”44 The Maryland OPC complaint provides a needed avenue to address

and remedy this ongoing misallocation and to protect existing customers from paying costs that

should be paid by large load customers. It is significant that large load data center developers and

 operators themselves acknowledge the importance of not assigning their costs to existing

customers. 45

         State public utility commissions also recognize the importance of fairly assigning these

costs, but they face an uphill jurisdictional battle in re-assigning costs shifted between transmission

customers. The Federal Power Act grants FERC exclusive jurisdiction over “the transmission of

electric energy in interstate commerce…[and] over all facilities for such transmission nor sale of

electricity.” 46 State regulation that “aims” at correcting problems arising in the transmission

system are certain to face scrutiny. 47 In Illinois, ComEd has argued that the Illinois Commerce

Commission “cannot reallocate transmission costs between ComEd and other [Load Serving

Entities] without effectively attacking the underlying FERC-jurisdictional rate design.” 48 While

the IL OAG believes there may be some paths to mitigate cost shifting that fall within the state

jurisdictional, 49 the fix is imperfect as long as there is a fundamental need to shift cost between

transmission customers as opposed to between retail ratepayers taking service under a single LSE.

II.      Maryland OPC’s proposal properly allocates risk to large loads, but it is limited by
         current FERC pricing policy.

         Maryland OPC’s proposal is grounded in FERC’s solution to interconnecting generators.

Order 2003 requires interconnecting generators to pay upfront for the incremental cost of

interconnection service, but that payment is then credited against the embedded cost of service.50

 These “but-for” interconnection costs are “not intended to be the means by which the Transmission

Provider recovers the cost of Network Upgrades.”51 Instead, the upfront payment is intended to be

a financing mechanism that is credited against “the higher of an embedded cost rate, or an

incremental rate designed to recover the cost of the Network Upgrades.” 52 FERC has noted that

by financing the incremental cost upfront and crediting against a “higher of” rate, “other

transmission customers…will not subsidize” the Interconnection Customer.53 FERC noted that

this rule “plac[ed] the Interconnection Customer initially at risk for the full cost of the Network

Upgrades,” but that this was necessary to incentivize the interconnecting generator “to make

efficient siting decisions and, in general, to make good faith requests for Interconnection

Service.” 54 This rule puts the onus on the interconnecting generator: continue to use the system or

lose the transmission credit resulting from the incremental connection cost.

       In arguing for a similar approach to be applied to large load interconnections, Maryland

OPC’s proposal is grounded in two separate but related concepts: “but for” costs and “higher of”

pricing. “But for” costs refer to the “upfront network upgrade costs not required ‘but for’” 55 the

interconnecting generator’s request for service. “But for” costs include the incremental cost (the

transformers and transmission lines necessary for service), as well as, if included in the rate base,

the return that the transmission owner receives on those assets.

       “Higher of” pricing is a reference to FERC’s requirement that transmission owners must

choose to charge either the embedded cost or incremental cost of service to those seeking service.

Generally speaking, the costs for transmission service can be divided into two buckets: embedded

costs and incremental costs. Embedded costs refer to the cumulative cost of existing infrastructure

 of the transmission grid, which in turn are the bases of the transmission revenue requirement.56

Incremental costs refer to the cost of the marginal infrastructure required to provide a new

customer with transmission service. 57 In Order 2003, FERC authorized transmission owners to

charge the “higher of” these two costs, under the rationale that for a given interconnecting

generator, the embedded cost and transmission cost reflect charges for the same service.58

Transmission owners can charge the “higher of” the embedded cost “or” the incremental cost.

        Maryland OPC’s proposes to treat large loads analogously to generators under Order 2003.

Maryland OPC argues that FERC “should adapt [the use of ‘but for’ and ‘higher of’ protections

from the merchant generator context] to the specific circumstances of data centers and large loads

seeking interconnection.”59 This allocation method would require “100 percent of the upfront

network upgrade costs not required ‘but for’ the large load additions” to be paid for by the large

load. 60 Those incremental costs would be credited against the large load’s usage of the entire

system, resulting in a discounted embedded cost rate for the large load for the depreciable life of

the incremental assets. 61

       Maryland OPC’s proposal resolves the threat of cost shifting between zones. It does so

because this proposal requires that incremental costs are covered by an agreement with the

transmission owner, transmission customer, and large load. There is no place for costs to escape

out of the zone because the proposal requires that both the incremental and embedded costs be

paid directly to the transmission owner of the relevant zone where the upgrades take place.

          The proposal also mitigates the risk of cost shifting among customers within a zone because

it eliminates the threat of stranded assets and encourages efficient decisions around data center

construction. As noted above, speculative interconnection requests and uncertainty in load

forecasting is a growing, and costly, problem. 62 Requests for interconnection that either fail to

materialize or that take less demand than what was expected directly increase the transmission

revenue requirement and the NITS rate for all other customers. 63 Under Maryland OPC’s

recommended approach, large loads will face their highest transmission costs at the beginning of

their life as they pay the incremental cost. By requiring the incremental cost to be paid upfront, the

risk of under-utilization, or even potential insolvency, is shifted onto the data center rather than be

shouldered by existing customers. Large loads will be forced to take a hard look at their costs and

potential revenue, resulting in more efficient siting decisions. 64

         Thus, Maryland OPC’s proposed remedy would treat many of the symptoms of PJM’s

existing unjust and unreasonable cost allocation, but it would stop short of addressing the

underlying cause. No cost allocation methodology can meet the challenge posed by large load

customers unless and until it recognizes that such customers are causing identifiable and

extraordinary incremental costs, and that they are relying on and benefitting from the existing

transmission network, including the historical and ongoing capital investment and expenses

necessary to maintain it. 65 As a result, a just and reasonable approach to transmission pricing would

allocate both the incremental costs attributable to a large load customer and the embedded cost of

III.     In order to prevent cost-shifting, FERC must revisit its prohibition on “and” pricing.

         FERC must revisit its stance on so-called “and” pricing in order to fully protect ratepayers

from paying for transmission costs caused by large load data centers. Under FERC’s policy against

“and” pricing, FERC has prohibited pricing that would “add an embedded cost rate to an

incremental cost rate for the same service over the same facilities.” 66 FERC can do so by

acknowledging that the rationale for its prohibition on “and” pricing is not applicable to large

loads.

         The context and reasons for which the prohibition on “and” pricing were starkly distinct

from today’s transmission landscape. In 1991, Penelec, a distribution utility subsidiary of First

Energy, attempted to charge a new, interconnecting generator both the “embedded costs of

Penelec’s transmission system” as well as a separate charge “designed to recover the costs

associated with actual reductions in economic energy transfers to Penelec’s native-load customers

resulting from the use of Penelec’s transmission system to accommodate the transmission of [the

generator’s] capacity and energy.”67 This “opportunity cost” reflected the cost that Penelec lost by

giving capacity to the independent generator. FERC ruled that this agreement was unjust and

unreasonable. The opportunity cost of not having capacity on transmission lines, the embedded

cost of continued system usage, and later, the incremental cost of building new transmission

infrastructure to accommodate the generator, were found to be a measure of the same service: the

limited transmission capacity in a transmission owner’s territory. Subsequently, FERC found that

         The prohibition on “and” pricing was grounded in two motivations: encouraging

competition among generators and ensuring that interconnection customers did not pay twice for

the same service. The first point is clear given the case in which this policy first arose. Penelec

attempted to leverage its market power as a transmission owner to maintain its control over

generation within its territory. In a pre-Order 888 world, FERC adopted this policy as “a useful

prophylactic to deter and prevent anticompetitive abuse.” 70 The second motivation follows from

the first, but is a desirable goal in its own right. It is a general principle in utility regulation, and

was specifically noted in Penelec, that a utility ought to provide “the lowest reasonable cost-based

rate” for a service. 71 Charging a customer more than the cost of service, for example by double

counting costs, would be contrary to that goal.

         These motivations are not applicable to large loads. As to competition among generators,

large loads are not generators. “Large-load customers are not competing with a utility in any way,

and utilities have no incentive to ‘artificially restrict the supply of transmission’ to large load

customers.” 72 But even supposing large loads were in the same position as independent generators

or could be coerced into paying monopoly rents to transmission owners in 1992, there have been

numerous regulatory developments since then. Most straightforwardly, Order 888 requires

transmission owners to provide open access transmission service, which includes non-

        The concern for large loads paying twice for the same service is equally inapplicable. As

noted above, large loads pay for two different benefits: (1) it takes services that are provided by

the existing transmission grid, 74 and (2) it requires marginal transmission expansion needed for

service to reach them. These services are unlike interconnection service for generators because in

that instance, the sole service being sold is access to the markets. Large loads are seeking access

to the transmission network, with the numerous benefits that it entails, and access to electricity

supply (i.e., the commodity) as well.

        Unlike “or” pricing, “and” pricing would allow transmission owners to charge both the

embedded cost and the incremental cost of service. Rather than a customer paying for the same

service twice, this would ensure that a large load customer is charged with the full cost to actually

serve it. Appropriately charging for both benefits will eliminate cost shifting among consumers.

Unlike the “higher of” pricing policy, large loads would pay their incremental costs, but they would

not receive a credit against their embedded cost rate.

                                             CONCLUSION

           The IL OAG supports Maryland OPC’s efforts “to ensure all Americans and domestic

industries have access to affordable, reliable, and secure electricity.” 93 Maryland OPC correctly

identifies the unjust cost shifting of massive transmission investments in PJM as they relate to

baseline transmission projects. To that end, the IL OAG calls on FERC to:

       •   Require transmission owners to directly allocate the incremental and embedded costs to

           large loads;

       •   Require PJM, the relevant transmission owner, the Eligible Customer taking service on

           behalf of a large load, and the large load to enter into a Cost Recovery Agreement;

       •   Adopt FirstEnergy’s proposal to disaggregate the incremental and embedded cost and

           assign both large load customers causing such costs;

       •   Permit “and” pricing in the large load context insofar as it captures all the services that a

           large load takes via connecting to the grid and prevents cost shifting among transmission

           customers; and

       •   Apply these suggestions to all transmission projects, not just baseline projects.
